title: The Burlington Arrives
body:
The arrival of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad in 1864 changed the scale of life in Downers Grove. A farming settlement could now exchange goods and passengers with Chicago along a regular rail corridor. The Main Street stop became an organizing point for the village: shops, streets, houses and everyday journeys gathered around the tracks. The railway was both a connection to the city and a reason for a town center to develop here.

That change did not begin on empty ground. The Encyclopedia of Chicago describes a community of farming families already established around the grove. Samuel Curtiss laid out a subdivision in 1863, the year before the railroad arrived. The settlement incorporated as a village in 1873. Reading those dates together shows a sequence of land development, transportation investment and local government, rather than a town created in a single dramatic moment.

The railway also helps explain the shape of the wider community. Growth developed near the Main Street, Belmont and East Grove stations. A rail siding and access to Chicago later made Downers Grove a destination for mail-order houses supplied by Sears, Roebuck & Co. between 1908 and 1940. Building materials and commuters moved along the same corridor, connecting domestic life with a much larger regional economy.

Passenger traffic eventually needed a different arrangement from freight handling. In 1911 a new passenger station replaced the original depot, which continued as a freight facility before being demolished. The Historical Society identifies the surviving building as Classical Revival with Beaux Arts influences. Its symmetrical front, pilasters and terra-cotta detailing belong to a station built almost half a century after the line arrived. Damage from the 1947 train wreck led to repairs using original bricks, giving the building itself evidence of successive periods of use and rebuilding.

title: Built for the Talkies
body:
When the Tivoli opened on Christmas Day in 1928, cinema was undergoing a fundamental change: recorded speech and music were becoming part of the film itself. The Downers Grove Historical Society identifies the theatre as an early building designed specifically for talking pictures. Local audiences came here to experience a new kind of entertainment in a setting intended to make a night at the movies an occasion.

The project belonged to local businessmen Gustav and George Bunge, a father and son. Van Gunten and Van Gunten designed the building, and J. T. Schless handled construction. The Historical Society records that thousands of people lined up for the opening program, which included Howard Hawks's film Fazil. The opening date places the building in the prosperous final years of the 1920s, before the economic upheaval of the following decade.

The theatre was only one part of the development. Bowling, commercial storefronts, offices and a residential hotel shared the building. That mixture matters to its history: the Tivoli was conceived as a downtown destination with several uses, rather than an isolated auditorium. Entertainment, work and lodging occupied the same block, helping to keep activity in the village center after daytime business had ended.

Later restoration and equipment changes allowed the Tivoli to remain a working cinema. The large main auditorium survived while many older theatres were subdivided into smaller rooms. A second, much smaller auditorium was added in 2021. The building's history is therefore not a story of everything remaining exactly as it was in 1928; it is a record of adapting a historic venue for successive generations of audiences.

The building has also provided a stage for live performance and community events. The Historical Society lists concerts by artists including Los Lobos, Neko Case and The Wallflowers alongside its account of film exhibition. That range of activity continues the original idea of a downtown entertainment destination. The theatre, its surrounding commercial spaces and the people using them connect the architecture with the village's cultural life.

title: A School Site Becomes a Gathering Place
body:
Fishel Park's open lawn has a history that predates the concert pavilion. In 1912, a kindergarten opened on Grove Street just west of Main Street, on the site now occupied by the park. The village's architectural and historical survey connects that school with the institution that later became the Avery Coonley School. The archival picture on this page shows the former school, not the present-day pavilion.

The early school formed part of a movement to take young children's learning seriously in its own right. The institution began here as the Kindergarten Extension Association School. Its program later expanded beyond kindergarten, and the building became known as the Junior Elementary School. Children learned at this downtown site before the school moved to its later campus. The building pictured in the archival view no longer stands.

Today, the Park District describes Fishel as a 1.9-acre park on the north side of Grove Street. The lawn, mature vegetation, play area and picnic spaces make it a shared outdoor room within the business district. The Veterans Memorial Pavilion provides a setting for the Summer Concert Series and other community events. The continuity is in the use of this land for public life, even though its buildings and activities have changed.

Remembrance is another layer of the park's history. The Historical Society documents a memorial to Downers Grove serviceman Tim Bodden, whose helicopter crashed in Laos in 1967. A plaque from an earlier memorial was relocated to Fishel Park in 1989. It was removed during pavilion construction in 2010 and subsequently returned. That account connects the recreational landscape to a family's long search for answers and the community's effort to remember its missing service members.

The school's early growth adds another chapter to that public history. Lucia Morse led the kindergarten that opened in 1912. In 1916 the program expanded to include first grade and took the name Junior Elementary School; additional grades followed in the 1920s. The archival photograph preserves a building that has disappeared, while the location remains available for shared activities. Its school history helps explain why an image of a classroom building belongs beside the later stories of concerts and remembrance at this park.

title: Israel and Avis Blodgett and the Underground Railroad
body:
The 1846 house at the museum campus belonged to Israel and Avis Blodgett, abolitionists whose home offered shelter and help to people escaping slavery. Its history connects an ordinary domestic building in Downers Grove with a much wider struggle over freedom, law and human rights. The National Park Service identifies the house as a station on the Underground Railroad, with the family's activity likely extending from the early 1840s until Israel's death in 1861.

The Blodgetts came from Massachusetts and established a farm and blacksmithing business in the area. Their house replaced an earlier log cabin. Its simple Greek Revival form belongs to the period when settlers were building more permanent homes, but architecture alone does not explain its significance. The important history also concerns what the family did inside the house and the assistance they provided beyond it.

The National Park Service cites first-hand accounts from the Blodgetts' children and a daughter-in-law, as well as a contemporary antislavery newspaper. Those sources describe aid and shelter at the family home and secret nighttime transport toward the home of Philo Carpenter in Chicago. The house was accepted into the National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom in 2023. This is a documented association, rather than simply a local tradition awaiting its first supporting evidence.

The house has also had a history of relocation and preservation. It was moved when Charles Blodgett built a later family home in 1892, and it returned to the museum campus in 2008 after a preservation campaign. The building's survival required decisions made long after the events for which it is remembered. Visiting it today means encountering both a nineteenth-century home and the result of a modern effort to preserve evidence of that past.

title: The Charles Blodgett House Becomes a Museum
body:
Two Blodgett houses tell different stories on the museum grounds. Charles Blodgett, the youngest son of Israel and Avis, built his own home here in 1892. The earlier 1846 house is associated with his parents and the Underground Railroad. The later house belongs to the next generation of the family and to a village that had already been reshaped by the railroad.

Charles combined local public service with agricultural business. The Historical Society's account describes his dairy operation and his long service on the DuPage County Board of Supervisors. His house was one of the larger homes built as residents expanded and modernized Downers Grove. Treating the two buildings as separate historical objects helps explain the change in both family circumstances and the surrounding community over the intervening decades.

The later house had another public life before becoming a historical museum. During the mid-twentieth century, owner Martin McGowan displayed taxidermied animals collected during his travels and admitted groups to see them. The Historical Society records that use as a distinctive episode in the building's history. It should not be confused with the museum's present interpretation of local history.

The Park District and Historical Society subsequently worked together to make the house a community museum during the 1970s. The Historical Society's timeline records its public opening in the 1892 house on January 30, 1977. Today the permanent exhibits interpret domestic life around the end of the nineteenth century, including the work and objects associated with a Victorian household. The campus also contains the Montrew Dunham History Center, which accommodates temporary exhibits and an interpretation of the local fire department.

The museum also keeps evidence that can help residents investigate their own part of the village's story. Its research library includes census records, cemetery surveys, genealogical material, newspapers, telephone directories and school yearbooks. That work extends the use of the site beyond touring furnished rooms. Buildings, collections and documentary records now share the former family property, making it a place for both interpreting local history and researching questions that remain open.

title: The Twin-City Zephyr Crash
body:
On April 3, 1947, the Twin-City Zephyr passenger train collided with a tractor near the Main Street station in Downers Grove. The tractor had fallen from a freight car moving on an adjacent track. The collision killed two passengers and a train-service employee. The Interstate Commerce Commission's investigation also recorded injuries among passengers and several members of the train crew.

The Zephyr was approaching Chicago from Minneapolis when the accident occurred. The local Historical Society describes the locomotive catching fire, the first two coaches jackknifing and the station being severely damaged. The event placed a long-distance passenger service, a freight movement and the village's everyday station in the same chain of consequences. The site was recognized through the Historical Society's historic-sites program in 1997.

The federal investigation reached a specific conclusion about cause. Its report, dated May 26, 1947, attributed the accident to freight being operated with a load that was not properly secured. That finding is more precise than describing the wreck simply as a collision at a station. The tractor was freight in transit, and its movement out of a freight car created the obstruction encountered by the passenger train. The commission investigated alongside a representative of the Illinois Commerce Commission.

The report places the collision at about 10:40 p.m. in misting weather. The passenger train was moving east on one track and the freight train west on the adjacent track. Investigators recorded that a signal displayed a proceed indication as the passenger train approached. The fireman saw the obstruction and called a warning as the engineer moved the brake valve to emergency. The locomotive and cars derailed, and coaches struck the station area. These recorded details show how quickly an unsecured load on one train endangered people on a neighboring track, even within a signal-controlled railway.

title: Morning Platform
body:
The Main Street platform belongs to a commuter corridor with roots in the nineteenth century. Metra's history of the BNSF line places the beginning of Chicago, Burlington & Quincy suburban passenger service in the 1860s. The Historical Society dates the original Downers Grove station to 1864, when it served a community whose agricultural business also benefited from the new railroad.

A commuter station connects two scales of life: the local streets around its platforms and the much larger city at the other end of the journey. In Downers Grove, that connection helped define the village center. The station's history is consequently about daily movement as well as famous trains or individual accidents. Repeated trips to work and home made the railway an enduring part of how residents used the village.

The equipment and companies carrying those trips changed over time. Metra's historical account describes the introduction of a fully dieselized locomotive fleet and stainless-steel, two-level passenger coaches in the early 1950s. The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy became part of Burlington Northern in 1970. The later merger with the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe in 1995 created the BNSF Railway. Those corporate names trace changes in the rail system rather than separate beginnings for the place itself.

The accompanying photograph was taken by David Wilson in May 2004. It shows the station in the era of Metra commuter service and makes the relationship between platforms, tracks and surrounding town visible. It does not establish today's timetable, fares or passenger numbers. Those operational details change and should be checked with the operator before travel.

The station building carries part of that history in its fabric. The present passenger station dates from 1911 and replaced the original 1864 depot. The Historical Society describes its symmetrical front, pilasters and terra-cotta details as features of Classical Revival design influenced by the Beaux Arts tradition. Repairs after the 1947 accident reused original bricks while some decorative trim was lost. The platforms and building have therefore served successive railway companies and generations of passengers through changes that remain visible at the site.
